a: Yes. MIT licensed, free and open source, commercial use welcome with no restrictions. HIDMaestro will never become paid, freemium, or Patreon early-access paywalled.

q: Do I need to enable test-signing mode?
a: No. Standard profiles use UMDF2 with a locally trusted certificate. The bundled USB/IP kernel packages retain their upstream Microsoft signatures. The SDK does not enable Windows test-signing mode.

Composite Sony, Valve and Nintendo profiles install the bundled usbip-win2 0.9.8.1 transport on a machine that has none. As of v2.0.1 that is its host controller alone: the SDK never runs usbip-win2's installer or installs its root-hub filter, so no USB device drops. Standard profiles use the Windows UMDF2 stack. A machine HIDMaestro put on 0.9.7.7 or 0.9.7.5 is moved to 0.9.8.1 automatically, with no window and no USB device dropping, so there is nothing to do when updating.

q: Can I add a controller you don't ship?
a: Yes, without touching code. Write a data-only JSON profile, or point HMDeviceExtractor at a controller you have plugged in and get a ready-to-deploy profile back.

q: How is this different from ViGEmBus, vJoy, or VIIPER?
a: Those tools install kernel drivers and present a small set of fixed device types. HIDMaestro runs in user mode and presents the exact identity of the profile you pick, 337 of them, down to the bus type, and adding a device means writing JSON rather than driver code. VIIPER additionally routes input through a network stack even for local play. The full comparison table above puts the tools side by side.

Yes. Steam recognizes the virtual controllers as the hardware their profiles declare, and the Valve personas go further: Steam files them under its own hardware, with the regression battery starting the actual Steam client to prove it claims and classifies all three.

q: Can two programs that embed HIDMaestro run on one machine?
a: Yes, as of v2.0.0. Each program keeps its own controllers, identities and sections, and a sweep removes only what exited programs left. The one exception is the remove-everything cleanup, RemoveAllVirtualControllers(HMCleanupScope.Everything, ...), which an uninstaller or a support tool calls. The driver is deployed by one program at a time and never downgraded, and the 2.0.0 driver is installed over any older one, whatever runs on it. A running program built on v1.12.0 or older still removes every HIDMaestro device on the machine at its InstallDriver and at its first create, and while one runs, a v2.0.0 program's controllers take transport indices from 64. Programs built on HIDMaestro 1.x must move to 2.0.0.

q: How do I remove HIDMaestro from a computer?
a: As of v2.0.1, run HIDMaestroUninstall.exe from the release ZIP. --preview lists what would go and changes nothing, and --yes removes without asking. A program that embeds HIDMaestro calls HMUninstall.Run() instead, from its own uninstaller or a settings button. A removal refuses while another program that embeds HIDMaestro runs, and other programs install the driver again at their next InstallDriver or create. With --include-usbip it also takes what usbip-win2's own installer left, its root-hub filter included, which restarts every USB 3 root hub. Windows' own logs and the GameInputSvc start type stay, and the report says why.

q: Does it work in NativeAOT and single-file apps?
a: Yes, as of v2.0.0, for NativeAOT and for trimmed, self-contained, single-file apps, on x64 and ARM64. The battery runs the two apps for the machine's architecture, so the ARM64 apps are built and published and have not run on ARM64 hardware.

q: Does the GameCube adapter work with Dolphin and Slippi?
a: Yes. The gamecube-adapter profile is Nintendo's WUP-028 on the USB/IP transport, and BindWinUsb() binds WinUSB to the virtual adapter so Dolphin and Slippi open it through libusb with no Zadig step. Their own adapter code, compiled unmodified, reads all four ports. The official SDL3 build for Windows has no libusb and lists no adapter, real or virtual.

Yes. Use v1.9.1 or later. One HIDMaestro.Core.dll serves x64 and ARM64 and carries a native driver payload for each, and the release has an ARM64 ZIP with an ARM64 test app and profile extractor. The ARM64 payload builds and is signed, and the battery builds its driver catalog on every run. No ARM64 machine has run the battery yet.
